newsitem.title: USA: Futures common banking seen step to consolidation.
newsitem.headline: Futures common banking seen step to consolidation.

text.p: - Common banking among U.S. futures exchanges may be a first step toward common clearing, in a process that could eventually lead to widespread industry consolidation, some futures industry officials said Friday.

Many industry sources said the common banking letter of intent announced this week at a Futures Industry Association (FIA) conference here was at least a symbolic move toward the goal of common clearing.

"I think that what you're going to see is a merging of the back office operations of many of the exchanges," said Charles Minnaar, senior vice president of marketing for the New York Cotton Exchange. "I think that makes a lot of sense."

Common banking would enable firms that do business on each exchange to effect settlement of their trades with a single transaction through common account at a bank, officials said. Under the agreement, each firm that is a clearing member of more than one exchange would be able to consolidate banking transactions.
"What this suggests is this is a precursor to other areas," Minnaar said. "I think there are mergers in the offing."
Leo Melamed, chairman emeritus of the Chicago Mercantile Exchange, characterized the common banking agreement as the first step in standardizing the U.S. futures industry.
"Yes, it's a precursor to common clearing and it's the first major achievement" in merging operations of exchanges, Melamed said.
NYCE's Minnaar said the industry was shifting to a more realistic, cost-conscious environment.
"You have to think about what exchanges are really offering, which is fundamentally a location," Minnaar said. Common economic sense dictates sharing duplicated responsibilities, he said.
Industry sources said much of the pressure to pursue common banking and clearing comes from futures commission merchants who use the exchanges.

Whether sharing physical space or banking and clearing operations, exchanges should look at practical approaches to saving money, agreed Joe O'Neill, NYCE president. He noted that the NYCE already uses the Board of Trade Clearing Corp for its computer clearing functions.
"NYCE felt it didn't have to reinvent the wheel," O'Neill said. As for common banking, he said, "This is the first step in one clearing corporation for the whole industry."
But some officials noted the common banking initiative, while symbolic for the U.S., was still in its infancy.
"What happened here yesterday is we signed a letter of intent to look at a concept," said John Hiatt, BOTCC president. "Whether we can get there, it's too early to tell," he said.

Several U.S. clearing organization officials said finalized details of a common banking agreement were still at least a year away. One New York exchange official noted similar letters of intent were signed by the CME and BOTCC last August and by the CME and the New York Mercantile Exchange in 1994.
"So this is not a new idea and it hasn't really gone anywhere," he said.

And even if the banking agreement can be hammered out in the next year and move forward, some said a common clearing agreement in the U.S. was bound to be more difficult to achieve. In common banking, exchanges will not share fiduciary risk, but in common clearing, fiduciary responsibilities may have to be shared by the exchanges.

Still, CME's Melamed noted that common banking fulfills the first goal of the Chicago Joint Strategic Initiatives Committee which was formed last year to investigate cost savings by consolidating parts of the two big Chicago exchanges.

"Actually, (committee chairman) Merton Miller put that as the number one goal to start with the basic mission, and we consider it to be the precursor to every other form of common (endeavor) whether it's processing or clearing."
Officials have set no target date for common clearing between the Chicago exchanges.

The seven U.S. clearing organizations representing U.S. futures exchanges that signed the letter of intent to begin common banking are: CME, BOTCC, NYMEX, the Commodity Futures Clearing Corp of New York, the Commodity Clearing Corp, the Kansas City Board of Trade Clearing Corp and the Minneapolis Grain Exchange.
